speechtext:
An answer or rather a comment made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) on the first motion called this afternoon impels me to bring to the attention of the House a practice into which the government have fallen, and which, I think, is not in compliance with a proper procedure or, indeed, at all a dignified treatment of parliament. I refer to the practice of permitting motions to pass, and then not complying with them as passed. I am not asking that all the information called for by this motion, for example-and others may be used equally well as examples-should be brought down, I am not arguing that the motion itself as written should pass; but I do say that if the government permit the motion to pass then they should comply with its requirements. If the government feel that the motion should not pass they should take the responsibility of specifically amending it, or making a definite reservation-no other course, to my mind, is justified. There have been cases where motions have passed this House calling for the production of certain information, the government not taking the responsibility of objecting. They permitted the motions to pass but took no responsibility; then, when the return was made the government said it was not in the public interest to give the information asked for. It is unnecessary to add that this is merely treating parliament with contempt. The government, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, should take their stand on each motion on its merits. If they desire to have the motion amended they should take the responsibility; and then when the motion passes it should be complied with in the form in which it passes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, May 2, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment there* to of Mr. Woodsworth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement of the Acting Minister of Finance has been justly praised for its clearness and brevity. The statement brings directly before us for consideration the most difficult of Canadian problems, a problem which must sooner or later be settled and settled rightly, or the consequences will be most disastrous. It has been said that the proposals mentioned involve a very direct departure from the policy which has hitherto prevailed. Assuming that to be correct, it is necessary for us to consider whether or not the proposals are consistent with the expressed will of the people and if so whether they are wise in themselves. The minister makes a number ol specific proposals in the way of reduction of taxation, and then states the general principle upon which he has proceeded. We are not at present concerned so much about the specific proposals as about the general principle. This general principle he has stated towards the end of his remarks, and as it has not been quoted for several days I will take the liberty of again reading it. The Acting Minister of Finance said, as reported at page 1218 of Hansard:
We have certain basic industries, upon the success o! which depend the growth of all other industries, and the greater development of our trade. Of these basic . industries, I would place agriculture, in all its varied branches, first. Next to agriculture, I would place our forests, our minerals and our fisheries. A real national policy is a policy that will encourage the growth and development of these basic industries.
And then, Sir, a little lower down the Acting Minister of Finance is reported to have said:
In that belief, Sir, we submit to-day proposals to lighten the burden of taxation on these primary basic industries.
Now, let us inquire whether the policy thus proposed is or is not consistent with the will of the people. During the election campaign of 1921, and indeed for a number of years before that the Liberal party-both inside of the House and out-proclaimed their

The Budget-Mr. Hudson
adherence to a policy of lowering the tariff, and particularly on the implements of production of the basic industries. That policy was very distinctly outlined in a resolution which was proposed to the House by the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) in the session of 1919. He was then supported not by all the Liberal members' but a great majority of them. In 1919 the supporters of the Liberal party met in convention and adopted a platform which incorporated that principle. Again in the session of 1920 and the session of 1921 resolutions were presented to the House, and supported by practically all of the Liberal members, and they involved the same principle. So much for the Liberal party. Now, the Progressive party who presented themselves for the first time in the election of 1921 were even more emphatic in their demands for a lowering of the tariff, and they too paid special attention to the duties on the implements of production. The Conservative party took the attitude which they still take. They are consistent in taking the view that a protective policy is vital to the interests of Canada, and it is not unfair to say that before the people at that election they were regarded as a high protectionist party; they might disclaim that but they were so regarded by the electorate. Now, at this election, a few more than two millions of people voted for the Liberal and Progressive candidates combined, and a few less than one million voted for the Conservative candidates. It would not be fair to say that all of those who voted for Liberal candidates approved of the declared policy of the party, because as we have heard from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and as we may hear from several other members on this side, they expressly disclaimed any desire to disturb the existing tariff and either expressly or impliedly disclaimed approval of the Liberal platform. But there were not many of these members, as far as my knowledge goes, and in fact if we make a very generous allowance for the people who voted for candidates holding these views among the Liberal party, there would still be an immense majority of the electors who must be taken to have approved of a policy of lowering or obliterating the duties on implements of production in the basic industries.
The facts that I have stated seem to me to show beyond question that there is no lack of consistency in the action of the government so far as the will of the electors is concerned; in fact, I think that the government would have been liable to most
severe criticism if they had failed to proceed along the lines that they now propose to follow. When a government comes into office it is seldom able to fulfil all of its preelection promises, but in all good faith it is bound to do all in its power to implement all such promises as are of a fundamental character.
The merits of the proposals of the government have been subjected to a great deal of discussion. Most that can be said for and against them has been said, and very little is left open to me that has not already been touched upon. In the first place, I would like to make some reference to a number of letters which were read the other night by the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Stewart). He read letters which seemed to indicate that the manufacturers of the city of Hamilton were in a very depressed and unhappy condition, because they conceived that the present budget was going to destroy the industries of their city. A copy of the Hamilton Spectator of Friday, April 2o, has been placed in my hands. In this paper, which was published about two weeks after the budget was brought down, appears an article of considerable length, which reads in part:
New industries have decided to establish here. Industrial commissioner secures two for city.
And has prospects of landing some others.
Prospects brighter this year than for long time. Representatives of two other large manufacturing concerns, one an American company and the other a Canadian firm, were in consultation with Industrial commissioner, Kirkpatrick, yesterday afternoon, but while they were favourably inclined to Hamilton as a location for their industries, arrangements were not yet completed. One requires-
And so forth. I will not take up time reading the article, but it indicates that there are at least cross currents in the good city of Hamilton.
I would like to refer to another matter that has been mentioned by a number of hon. member? this year and last year-the statement that it is desirable that Canada should become a self-contained country. That statement has obtained certain currency throughout the country, perhaps because it has a highly patriotic flavour, but it seems to me that it is a vain hope, a futile desire, a rainbow which even the most optimistic can never hope to witness. If we look round the world for a country that enjoys this enviable condition we are met with some disappointments. Our thought would naturally first turn to Great Britain; that country is probably less self-contained than any other first-class nation in the world; she is dependent to a very large extent on the outside world for her food, and
The Budget-Mr. Hudson

to an even larger extent for her raw materials and for all sorts of things that enter into the life of the community. She lives by external trade. Never since she was -a nation has Great Britain been self-contained; and she never will be unless the day comes when Macaulay's vision of the New Zealanders' visit is realized. The next nation we might turn to is Imperial Germany. That country is probably the place where this conception of a self-contained nation was first fully developed. For over 40 years she strove, with all the aids of science, and with all the ingenuity, energy and persistency of her people, to become self-contained. After a few years, finding that her efforts were failing, she reached out to other parts of the world to acquire possessions which might provide all that she needed to use from within her own jurisdiction. The result of this policy contributed largely to bringing about the Great War, and it was because she was not self-contained that the Great War was concluded at as early a stage as it was.
Another country in Europe that might be considered is France. She is much more self-contained than most other nations, and- yet she is dependent on the outside world for a very large portion of her food, and for an even larger proportion of her raw material. She, too, is reaching out into the outside world trying to supplement what she lacks. The smaller nations of Europe such as Belgium, Holland, Denmark and Sweden, all depend to a very large degree on the outside world. So that in Europe there is no comfort to those who proclaim their wish that a country should become self-contained, and their belief that if it did become such it would be happy.
Turning to the United States, that country is probably more favoured by nature in the diversity of its climate, and in its natural products and its geographical position than any other country in the world. She too has sometimes thought that she might be self-contained, but the result is that she is importing more and more year by year. She sets up a high protective tariff against Canada, and yet notwithstanding that tariff each year sees an increase in.her imports from Canada. So that if we look over the whole world we do not find any civilized country which seriously attempts to be self-contained in this present year. It is said that the only people that are really self-contained are negroes of central Affrica, and even they trade coconuts, for calicoes.

Probably not. In Canada we have great natural resources and we are proud of them, but there are a great many things that we lack and a great man}' things that we cannot get along without. In 1879, when the so called National Policy was inaugurated, the fathers of that policy had this same idea of a self-contained nation. They said:	We will soon become great if we shut
out these industrial products from elsewhere and live within ourselves. The result of that policy, which has been in force ever since with a few modifications, has been that Canada has imported more and more, year by year, from that time. The truth is that no country can maintain its place in our advancing civilization without drawing largely on the outside world. As somebody said, to attempt to do so is a fruitless struggle against the spirit of the age. When you have free communications, free trade in literature, free trade in ideas, you cannot persuade people to do otherwise than insist on procuring material things from wherever they can get them to their liking. It seems to me that if we keep that in mind, the true policy is along the lines indicated by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in the latter part of his statement; we should turn our thoughts to the development of our resources where we have an advantage, to doing and making the things we can do and make better and more cheaply than anybody else. If we do that, we have ample resources to provide for the profitable employment of the energies of all of the people who are now here and all that we can hope to have for generations to come.
There is another matter which, perhaps, has not been referred to directly by any member during this debate, but which is mentioned sometimes in the press and sometimes on the street, and that is, retaliation. People complain, perhaps rightly, that we are sometimes dealt with unreasonably by the people of the United States or of other countries in regard to tariffs. It is not unnatural that a person who is injured by such a move should feel resentment and should ask for retaliation. But it seems to me that anything of this sort should be proceeded with very slowly, because it seldom happens that you can repair the injury to the injured person by retaliation. You may vent your feelings, but, except in rare cases, you do not benefit by retaliation. There is another reason why we should proceed very slowly with any idea of that sort, and that is this. The United States is a great nation, twelve times at least our size in

The Budget-Mr. Hudson
population and more than twelve times in wealth. We live side by side on a border of 3,000 miles, and to large extent our resources are complementary to theirs. We cannot get away from nature, and nature intended that we should live side by side in a neighbourly way. If we are going to do anything, I think our policy should be one of conciliation, and that, for the furtherance of such a policy, the government as soon as it possibly can, should get a competent representative at Washington and do all in its power to bring about better trade relationships with the United States.
One hon. member, I think the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), remarked that we could not afford in Canada to take our trade policy from either Great Britain or the United States. It seemed to me that there was a great deal of truth in that remark, but it also seemed to me that we could not afford to ignore any lessons which we might leam from what had happened in either of those countries, applying them to our own conditions. In the course of the debate quite a number of members have referred to the value of the home market. The argument has run something like this; Bring in more people, raise the tariff, stiffen it up a little bit; we shall have more people in the cities and industries flourishing, and then our farmers' troubles will soon disappear, because the people in the cities will eat and pay for what the farmers produce. This is a case where we might fairly look at what has happened in the United States before deciding on the validity of that argument. The United States, as all hon. members know, is a nation of over 100,000,000 people. It is highly industrialised, its industries, as a whole, are probably thirty or forty years in advance of ours-I mean in the extent to which they are industrialised. They have enjoyed the blessings of a highly protective policy for several decades, probably for generations; they have as many large cities as they can very well support; they have an urban population in the whole country greatly exceeding the rural population. That being the case, what is happening? During the last few years the agricultural population of the United States has fallen into distress, distress to the degree that they had to seek federal assistance and the federal government came to their aid, providing various methods, for instance agricultural credits, long-term credits, short-term credits, intermediate credits. All this was put in force, but while it may have helped, it did not cure the situation. The next thing that happened was this: The United States' farmers, unlike our farmers, have been educated to believe in the efficacy of a protective tariff. They think it is right, so they go to congress and ask congress to pass a law imposing a very high tariff, a prohibitive tariff, against the products of Canadian farmers. Congress accedes to their request and imposes what they thought was a prohibitive tariff. But that did not cure the situation; they found soon that that did not improve prices, it did not remedy their distress. The next step was a measure which is now before congress, probably being discussed there to-day, known as the McNary-Haugen bill. This bill, when I heard of it first, seemed to me to be a most fantastic production, a scheme which could hardly be hoped to work, or to be considered by thoughtful business men. To put the matter very shortly, those back of this McNary-Haugen bill argue thus: The troubles of our farmers arise because they hive an exportable surplus and the price of their products, of what they have to sell, is determined in a world market. The world market is a bad one at the present time, and we have to deal with it on that basis. So, we will form a government corporation having a capital of $200,000,000. That corporation will be empowered to ascertain what the amount of the home consumption of various agricultural commodities will be, then to take the exportable surplus and to sell it at the best price that can be secured in Europe, the government taking the loss. In the meantime the prices of these commodities are to be fixed in the United States by the rather curious procedure of ascertaining what the relative prices of agricultural products and other commodities were in 1914;-prices of farm products, that is to say, have not gone up, while other prices have gone up, and the relationship of these prices in 1914 will be found out-and, having ascertained that, they will then fix the prices for the domestic market on that basis; and in order to prevent that figure being disturbed, they will give to the President, under the advice of the commission, power:
To determine the rate of duty upon any agricultural commodity, or upon any derivative of or competitive substitute for such commodity, necessary to maintain or to assist in maintaining the domestic price of such commodity at the level of the ratio prices fixed therefor.
There are in the bill several sections which it may be of interest to this House to quote as disclosing the nature of the proposal, and the conditions which the United States legislators feel that they have to deal with. Section 21 reads:
It is hereby declared that there exists a general emergency in respect of agricultural commodities by reason of-

becomes of less significance? Adam Smith, who has already been referred to in this debate, predicted over a hundred years ago that England was coming to bankruptcy because of her over-borrowing. But Adam Smith did not know about the possibilities of steam, and he could know little about the advent of the industrial revolution, The effect of that industrial revolution was to change the ratio of wealth to such an extent-that is the ratio existing between the debt and wealth-that the debt became comparatively insignificant. Is there, I ask, any hope for the future that we may in any way change this ratio so that the public debt will bear much less heavily comparatively speaking, than it does at the present time? May I now suggest some things that we may do?
First of all we can take steps now to eliminate future wars. I suggest that that can be done by passing-not in the future, but now- a universal draft law that will mobilize not only wealth but men, so that in time of the nation's peril every fit man and woman will know that back of him or her in the effort to preserve the country is placed all the available wealth, every resource, and every activity of the country. In other words, to pool the country's resources of both men and wealth to meet the national peril, whatever it may be. I think that would take much of the profit out of war. The best way to prepare for war is to prepare for it in the piping days of peace. I think this method would effectively discourage war. That is the first thing that I suggest. We do need security against war for the future. Now is the time to obtain that security.
Now, what about this public debt? We pay little attention to it. It is pyramiding year after year. What are we going to do about it? Are we going to do anything until we are face to face with calamity? Well, several plans have been suggested, and I simply want to mention them here in passing. There are those who suggest that repudiation is the proper thing. Personally I do not think that is advisable. In the first place it would constitute a gross breach of faith towards those to whom we are under an obligation. It would not only raise interest rates to speculative figures but would shatter the confidence in this country held in other lands, and would invite confiscation of the property held by Canadians in foreign lands. It would necessarily destroy the whole fabric of our industrial life and, in addition, would invite international hostility.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Can my hon. friend say who, in Canada, suggests repudiation of the debt?
[Mr. Shaw.J

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not implying that anybody in Canada has suggested it. I have not heard it suggested here; as a matter of fact nothing whatever has been suggested here. But other countries are suggesting it, either inferentially or otherwise. Then there are others who propose that we should have a moratorium as far as our public debts are concerned, which, of course, is another although less obnoxious form of repudiation. There are those who suggest that the debt may be reduced by inflation; and then, of course, there is in England a very large group of people who are in favour of what they designate as a capital or a wealth levy. The Labour party of England declared that when they came to power they would bring into effect a capital levy for the purpose of reducing the public debt. That party is in office in England at the present time. In a capital levy there are several vital principles involved and various considerations of technique with which I am not going to deal. These are some of the plans suggested. There is another plan, and that is the one which we in Canada follow-that is do nothing at all. In this country we are sweating away on the treadmill under the delusion that we are mountaineering. That is our situation in Canada. I say: Why wait for opportunities, why not make the opportunity? Unfortunately our entire history is a melancholy record of not doing things in time. What can we do before events will force upon us the formulation of a policy which perhaps in that event will be ill-considered and hasty. I think we should follow the practice pursued in England at the present time and appoint a responsible committee which will investigate the public debt-not only investigate the debt itself but inquire into the incidence of the debt taxation itself, its effect upon employment, and the effect upon the nation's life generally. I think a necessary step if we want to deal with this matter intelligently is to appoint a responsible committee that can make full investigation into all the facts surrounding this important matter. It will at least give us the information. Then of course we should at the earliest possible date convert our loans at lower interest rates. It should be done.
Again there can be no doubt that we should learn to discipline expenditure, in order to secure results which amply justify our outlay. Further there is the question of the investigation of various taxation methods, suggested, I think, in the Speech from the Throne. I think it is highly desirable that we should investigate our taxation methods thoroughly, in order that we may bring to light the proper means for a debt reduction. In this connec-

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
tion I want to speak very shortly about one method of taxation, because it is referred to in the motion of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) and that is the Inheritance Tax. It is undeniable that during the war vast fortunes were made out of the nation's peril. It is also undeniable that those who made these vast fortunes gave no adequate return to the state. I speak not only of Canada but elsewhere. Now should these beneficiaries go longer without taxation? Should we call upon the workers and legitimate industries to bear a still larger share of the burden? To be perfectly frank, I do not think that wages or legitimate profits can bear any heavier taxation than is being imposed at the present time. If there is one principle upon which our property system depends, it is that a man is entitled to the property which he creates. That is the sound principle upon which our institutions stand to-day. But I want to point out to you, in the light of that principle, three questions in connection with this proposed method of taxation. First of all, what right has a deceased person to give property? Why should the founder of an estate bind or control a coming generation? One generation ordinarily cannot bind another. This parliament cannot bind another parliament which may follow. It makes its own laws. Can a father, presuming him to be the founder of an estate, bind his son to contribute in labour to the welfare of an individual or to the welfare of society? He cannot do it. Inheritance means that the founder of an estate compels society to feed, to clothe and to shelter the beneficiary whom he may nominate; and in that way a living generation is bound by the wishes of a wealthy deceased. On the other hand, if this is a good principle, why not ccmpel the son of an indigent father to pay his father's unpaid debts? That would undoubtedly be unfair to the son. If there is going to be inheritance, it would seem logical that there should be inheritance not only of assets but of debts; and if ancestors are to be obeyed, and if we pay respect to the wishes of wealthy ancestors, why not pay respect to the wishes of all ancestors, no matter who they may be? The government today should be by those who are not only physically but geographically present.
Then the second question, what right has the heir to receive? I have already suggested the principle that the title to property can only be morally based on the result of one's own effort. One has no right to property because his father earned it. The father is under obligation, of course, to maintain his son during the years of dependency, but no
further. Blood or kinship confers no merits whatsoever upon the claimant to an estate. It is not a natural right, because if it were society would insist on a father transferring his estate to the son. As a matter of fact it is left to the father's own volition. It is not a contract right, because in contracts there is always consideration moving from one party to the other. In this case the heir gets something for nothing. President Lincoln put the matter very clearly on one occasion when he said, "I have no right to any special privilege of receiving money without earning it, because I thus deprive another of part of what he has earned." A will is merely a direction, as I have already suggested, that the next generation shall support and feed and clothe and shelter the beneficiary according to the terms in the document itself. Again, suppose for instance, a penniless man should suddenly claim from society the right to live in receipt of a princely income, what would society do? Why such a claimant would be promptly sent off to some lunatic asylum. But suppose he produces a document signed by some wealthy deceased, then we honour it. You can see that the position is entirely illogical. Thirdly, why do people consent to this condition of affairs, if there is no right in the founder to give and no right in the heir to receive? Because the fact is that they do not understand the significance of the question, and the only way by which it could be brought to their attention would be if it should happen that all the wealthy deceased should die on the same day and all beneficiaries come into their property on the same day. Do hon. members think for a single moment that the rest of society would tolerate such a state of affairs? I think not. They would then realize how vain it would be to struggle against an economic status fixed for them before birth. There can be no doubt that this inheritance principle makes for concentration of wealth. It is a comparatively difficult matter to acquire a fortune. In these latter days, with tax exempt securities and bonds and similar securities, it is comparatively easy to retain and even to increase a fortune. Let me illustrate by reference to some figures from the United States the exact concentration which this represents. In 1913 there were 29 people in that country who held fortunes totalling 2,7o6 millions. They had yearly incomes of above 176 millions. In 1915 there were 7,509 people in the United States with fortunes totalling 33 billions. Suppose the United States government had handed a million dollars to each one of th6se families and taken the rest by inheritance taxation, it would have secured the sum of approximately
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

26 billion dollars, which it would obtain in the course of a generation, and which sum represents practically the same amount as the total expenditure of the United States government for the first 127 years of its history. The argument I suggest for the inheritance tax is incontrovertible. It cannot be successfully controverted, but there are those who say that the provincial governments levy such a tax. True it is they levy a tax. Let us compare the situation in the United tSates. I made some investigation of the problem last summer. I found, with the exception of two states-and they may have changed their minds since-that practically every state in the American union levies an inheritance tax, and they levy it on substantially the same basis so far as percentage is concerned as our Canadian provinces. But in addition to that, the federal government levies a very heavy inheritance tax. It exempts incomes up to $50,000, but after that it levies a tax which brings the maximum taxation, counting both state and federal, on one inheritance to something over sixty per cent on large estates. Now, if they can do that in the United States there is absolutely no reason why we cannot do it here. If the American states of the union and if the federal government can each levy an inheritance tax, there is absolutely no reason why we cannot do exactly the same thing. It is true it may not amount to much at the outset. It would at least involve very little expenditure, but it would make provision against the day when these tremendous estates fall by reason of the death of their holders and founders. It would be comparatively easy to collect, because all this government would have to do would simply be to make an arrangement for each provincial government to collect on a commission basis, or failing that for the federal government to levy the taxation through their already constituted Income Tax department. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that it seems to me that the argument for this system of taxation is incontrovertible. I think it should be instituted now in order to provide for the future. Not that I am hopeful that it will provide much revenue in the immediate future, but in days to come it will be of increasing significance, and from what source can we secure by taxation money which can more justly be applied to the reduction of our public debt? I shall not further weary members of the House by reference to this question of the public debt.
I want to deal now, and very shortly, with the fiscal proposals which have been proposed by the govemme'nt, to obtain during the coming year. The government propose several reductions, first by way of sales tax,

a general reduction of one per cent, on special articles a larger amount, and in some cases, articles are exempted altogether from the sales tax. With that reduction I have no quarrel whatsoever and I have no objection to it. Then the government propose certain tariff reductions on implements of industry, on the primary implements required in the development of our natural resources. I think that is highly advisable, highly desirable. If I had any complaint at all, it would be that the proposals do not go far enough.

speechtext:
If they do not reach the
farmer, all I can say is that the manufacturer will not be seriously hurt. But I am frank to say to the hon. gentleman, for whom I have the highest regard, that I am not in a position to say whether the full amount of that customs reduction will, either now or ultimately, reach the primary consumer. I may say, however, as is suggested to me by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), that there can be no doubt that the freight rates will reach the farmer immediately. I am not giving these figures because I object to the customs reduction. I do not want that impression to prevail at all. I want to give these figures to the House so that we may get a proper perspective of what relief we are receiving. Then I want to take time by the forelock and suggest to the government what the restoration of the Crowsnest pass agreement will mean to the primary producers.
There are a few matters that I want to speak about with regard to the tariff. My hon. friends to my right are fearful of this reduction. They have told us in no unmeasured terms about the difficulties under which Canada labours to-day. They have pointed to the exodus; they have specially urged that the manufacturing industries of this country have suffered very severely. I have taken the trouble to figure out a few computations from a comparison of income taxes paid during the fiscal years 1921-22 and 1922-23. This statement indicates that the agrarian portion of the population has suffered much more severely than the manufacturing portion of the population. It indicates that the number of agrarians paying income tax has lessened by more than one-half and that the decrease in the tax paid has varied on a per capita average from $89 to $57. It indicates that the number of manufacturers in Canada-I am speaking now about unincorporated	manufacturers-has
actually increased from 1,629 to 1,732 during that period, but there has been a substantial decrease in the income tax paid. If that means anything, it would, I suggest, mean that the manufacturers have not suffered comparatively more, but, as a matter of fact, have suffered comparatively less than other portions of the community. Then I ascertain from the figures that while there has been a substantial decrease in the number of manufacturing corporations paying income tax, there has not been anything like a comparative decrease in the percentage of income tax paid, because-and it may interest hon. members to know this-whereas in 192122 the average income tax paid by manu-facturine corporations in Canada was $7,602, a not inconsiderable item when you take into account the exemptions, this amount has been reduced to only $7,133 in the last fiscal year. Again, I have worked out in some detail the percentage of decreases in income tax payments in the various provinces of Canada between the years 1922 and 1923. I find that in the agricultural provinces there has been

The Budget-Mr. Shaw

a much larger decrease than in the manufacturing provinces. The decrease in Ontario is only 19.5 per cent, and in Quebec 20.7 but in Manitoba the decrease has been 34.3 per cent, in Saskatchewan 36 per cent, in Prince Edward Island 25 per cent and in Nova Scotia 28 per cent. These figures only illustrate, I think, that it is not primarily from lack of protection that the manufacturers suffer, but that they suffer perhaps on account of protection in common with, though to a less extent than, many other people in Canada.
I have been rather impressed with the arguments advanced by my protectionist friends who tell us about the dire distress that is experienced by the manufacturing industry, and 1 have taken the trouble to consult the Year Book. I may interject the remark here that this book is a veritable mine of information. I have looked up the percentage of the failures in Canada during the past year as compared with other years and I find that there has been only a comparatively small increase. This of course covers not only the manufacturing concerns but, as well, every variety of trader and merchant; and the interesting fact is that while the Year Book has classified the causes of failures, lack of protection, which we are told is an important cause for failures in Canada, is not taken into consideration at all by the Dominion Statistician. This is strange; but it is perfectly clear that the Dominion Statistician in his figures has taken no cognizance of the lack of protection as a cause for failures. If he has then all I can say is that, so far as the reasons for business failures in Canada are concerned, there does not seem to be any difference in percentage of failures as compared with the United States, that alleged highly protective country.
Hon. gentlemen to my right seem to be under the delusion that the United States tariff is the very acme of fiscal perfection, the thing for which we should strive, the thing towards which we should set our faces, rather than harking back to anything like free trade. The analysis of the percentage of goods, taking them by value, entered free into the United States and Canada discloses, however, a rather interesting fact, namely, that in the year 1922 61.43 per cent of goods imported into the United States entered free of duty whereas in Canada only 33 per cent of our imports entered free. Not only that, but the average percentage of duty on all imports into the United States was, for the year 1921, 11.44 per cent, and in 1922, 14.68 per cent, as against an average percentage of duty on all imports into
'Mr. Shaw.]
Canada of 14.1 per cent in 1921, 16.2 per cent in 1922, and 16.7 per cent in 1923. So that apparently, from that standpoint, we have a higher average percentage than the United States. Then, too, I find that in the year 1922 the United States, with a population of 110,000,000, collected 8456,000,000 by customs taxation whereas we in Canada collected $105,000.000 in other words, the United States in 1922 collected per capita $4.07 while we collected per capita $11.75. And the figures through all the years substantiate the facts I have given. In the United States they depend on customs taxation only to the extent of 10 per cent of the revenue, while in Canada we depend upon it to the extent of 30 per cent. I have taken the trouble to make up a list, only a few items of which I shall give, in relation to the American tariff. I find that shovels and spades, which are very necessary articles to a great many people, are imported into the United States subject to a tariff of 30 per cent whereas we in Canada impose against these articles a duty of 32^ per cent. Boots and shoes enter free into the United States, but we have a tariff on them of between 25 and 30 per cent.

speechtext:
The hon. member is referring to the recent reduction in'the budget. I have a note of it, and I regret that for his sake I did not mention the fact. To proceed: cement enters free into the United States as against a tariff of approximately 10 cents per hundred pounds when it is imported into Canada. Again, cowhide gloves, which are necessary for a great many labouring men, are imported free into the United States; when we import them into Canada we have to pay 35 per cent. Leather is imported free into the United States, but it pays a duty of 15 per cent in going into Canada. Sewing machines pay a duty on importation into the United States of 15 per cent.; when they are imported into Canada they are subject to a duty of 30 per cent. Harness and saddlery are in certain cases imported free into the United States, but they are subject to a duty of 30 per cent, when imported into Canada. Typewriters, which are used by a great many people, especially young people in earning a livelihood, are admitted free into the United States whereas they pay a customs duty of 25 per cent, when imported into Canada. And automobiles, which pay 25 per cent, in the

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
United States, are taxed 35 per cent, on importation into Canada. There are a great many more items in this list but I shall not weary the House by referring to them.
Now, there are those who suggest that the greatest necessity of the time is
5 p.m. stability in regard to the tariff. The present advocates of stability, condemned the government last year for not carrying put their pre-election promises, now they condemn them for making an attempt in that direction. What I suggest to my hon. friends to my right is that the policy of the government up to the presentation of the present budget has been substantially that bequeathed them by the late administration. But we cannot expect stability in this day and generation, at a time when the whole world is in a state of flux and change. Under these circumstances, it seems to me the height of absurdity to ask for stability in anything. In England about a year and a half ago a government was elected upon a policy of stability and tranquility. It lasted just a year; and the wonder is, not that it was elected but that it lasted so long. The voice of any one crying for stability or tranquility at the present time is simply the voice of an infant crying in the night, and with no language but a cry.
It is suggested by those who favour the protectionist theory that the policy is designed to develop industry, and create the fullest employment. If you ask the protectionist to give you some evidence of prosperity he hastens to the trade returns and rejoices if they indicate any increase over the previous year. But in asking for protection, or in desiring to place a protective barrier against importations, he finds himself on different ground, because if the tariff means anything it means the exclusion of imports and he consequently negatives the argument which he first suggested. It is quite apparent that imports depend upon exports and exports upon imports. I do not think anybody in this day and generation can controvert that statement. Payment for our exports must come by way of goods and services; it can come no other way. And if you limit exports of this country you necessarily clog the wheels of industry, you necessarily lessen employment in this country. No country can enrich itself by erecting a tariff barrier and so isolating itself commercially from the rest of the world. It does not in the long run benefit our own country to produce at excessive cost what another country can produce cheaply and more efficiently. It is idle to imagine that'it profits a country to allow manufacturing in-llli
dustry to take a certain toll from the people by reason of customs taxation which otherwise it would not be entitled to. So far as consumers are concerned, this constitutes legal spoliation. I would suggest that the tariff places a premium on incompetence and inefficiency, for the manufacturing industry which has to rely upon a protective tariff exploits citizens of its own community and therefore is necessarily inefficient and incompetent.
But if my hon. friends think the policy of economic isolation is a proper policy, why not apply it to every province; why not have every province isolate itself? Why not apply it also to every city, indeed to every hamlet? No one would suggest for a moment that such a policy would be desirable. There can be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that artificial interference with the natural flow of imports really narrows rather than expands markets. We want to-day expanded markets; that is our main requirement, A tariff policy cannot make for steady employment; it can. only give an artificial stimulus to industry. It increases the cost of living, and, more than that, it ^ is the worst and most exhausting form of raising public revenue, because with every increase in the tariff the manufacturer is able to exact just that much more from the unfortunate consumer. So, Mr. Speaker. I would suggest that a protective tariff is not justifiable, I care not if you take it on the ground of revenue, on the ground of the development of industry, or on the ground of increasing employment; and still less can it be justified, on the ground of common morality.
Now, surely fifty years' experience of this protective policy should be sufficient. For fifty long years we have followed this policy. For fifty years we have primed the pump of Canadian industry with this policy, designed at the outset for two purposes; first, to assist infant industries; and, secondly, to force reciprocity from the United States. It has miserably failed in both particulars, and only those engulfed in the quicksands of protection would for a single moment deny the fact.
Now, why do we tolerate this system? Is it because of the grip of selfish interests on this country? I think not, because I am satisfied that if the sunlight of fact were allowed to illumine the fiscal darkness even for a short time, these interests would be readily dispersed from their slender defence. Is it because the people believe in the policy? Surely not. Everybody is a consumer, and surely every-, body has learned by costly and bitter experience that this system does not profit them. It seems to me that one of the main reasons
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

for the continuance of protection is due to what I may call the more or less spineless attitude of those committed to the policy of free trade. Knowing the facts, inspired by sound principles, they have not hesitated, before election, to proclaim from the housetops their devotion to the principle; but their pre-election militancy and the urge to action seem to die with the declaration of their election. I do not know why it should be so, for it seems to me that there are enough free traders in this country now to serve notice upon our industrialists that we are going to give them reasonable time, perhaps five years -limit the time-to get down to a free trade basis, and that after that period has elapsed we shall insist upon free trade as the fiscal policy of the nation.
But there is another and very important reason, Mr. Speaker, why we should develop the free trade policy of this country. I am. thinking now particularly of the world situation. Despite rulers, despite parliaments, the people everywhere are gradually coming back, if I may say so, to their normal senses; there is observable in all parts of the world a restoration to sanity. When the common people of all the belligerent countries come into control and take charge of their affairs, they are going to find out the causes that make for war and prevent them from living in peace and harmony even with their own countrymen. I remember that one of the conditions of the Armistice, incorporated in the Fourteen Points, provided for the elimination of customs barriers. The late ex-President Wilson saw with a. very clear and statesmanlike vision that tariffs make for war. But unfortunately the peace of Versailles did violence to that condition. I say "unfortunately" advisedly, for under that peace, to-day the world has little chance. In deference, apparently to nationalistic sentiments that treaty set up ten additional nations in Europe. They promptly, as they fought for self-preservation, commenced to set up tariff barriers to protect themselves, presumably from their neighbours. Armaments necessarily followed, because militarism and protection always walk hand in hand and keep step with each other. So to-day as a result the whole industrial fabric of Europe is in ruins, and the tragic sacrifice, the awful suffering and the heroic endurance displayed in the last war have apparently been largely in vain.
But, as I suggested, there is some hope for the future. Let me give the House my reasons [DOT] for thinking so. Hungary, under the aegis of the League of Nations, has adopted free trade. England, the home of free trade, despite all her domestic difficulties and problems, and

despite the efforts of tariff propagandists, has recently reaffirmed the principle of free trade more strongly than ever. Not only that, but the neighbouring country of Ireland recently appointed a tariff commission which, after fully analysing the facts, came to the conclusion that free trade was the proper policy for Ireland to adopt. In addition, Russia, which has recently entered into the comity of nations again, is now making trade arrangements with the other countries of the world. These are hopeful signs. But not only on the continent of Europe are there signs of better times. Even in the country to the south I think the people are gradually awakening to the futility of their protective policy, and I am hopeful that in the coming presidential election they will see to it that steps are taken to cast this thing from their midst.
Now, Canada cannot do better than to set the pace for this movement. She occupies a particularly strategic position in the world to-day. I see no reason why she cannot take a step in advance of other nations.
I come now to speak particularly on the motion and the amendment which are before the House. The motion before the House is that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means. But that is really not what. is meant at all. I am sure there would not be a single one of us but would gladly give the Speaker an opportunity to leave the chair and escape from the present and future floods of language; I am sure of that. But it does not mean that at all. We have old forms and old fictions, and the real question we are asked to vote on in this motion is whether or not we approve of the government policy incorporated in the budget. That is the question we have to consider.
Then there was an amendment proposed by my- hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), which goes just a little bit further than the proposals of the government. The hon. member for Battleford (Mr. McConica), whom I see in his seat, is very, very sorry indeed that the Conservative amendment was not allowed, because that amendment provided for tariff stability and he wants a battle over that issue. Perhaps he may be pardoned for not knowing that in this country for the last fifty years that is the very issue we have been battling on, the issue of the tariff. It has been a sham battle through all these years, and it will continue in the future, as in the past, to be nothing more than a sham battle unless we get it put on a proper and a solid basis. But as I say, perhaps my hon. friend may be

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
pardoned, coming, as we know he does, from the republic to the south. I was interested in reading the remarks in Lord Bryce's book on the American Commonwealth, written twenty years ago, where he says that the Republicans and the Democrats in the United States have lost all vital differences, and that there is now only a struggle between them for power and position; party names, he say^ still persist, while principles and causes have vanished. And so as they have been having these sham battles over there, I presume my hon. friend from Battleford wishes to import them over here. For him to ask in this day and generation for the perpetuation of these sham battles of the past is to court the character of none other than Rip Van Winkle.
I come now to deal particularly with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg, and I would direct the attention of the House particularly to the preamble of his resolution. He says:
Whereas the budget proposals would seem to indicate the recognition by the government of the necessity for a fiscal policy designed to encourage industries based upon the development of the natural resources of the country, and to afford some alleviation of the financial burdens bearing upon the people;
In other words, he distinctly, if I understand the language at all, approves of the government policy to the extent that it has gone. Then he says:
And whereas the condition of such industries and tlie condition of consumers in general is such as to demand relief ;
Therefore be it resolved:-
That the best interests of Canada will be served by an immediate and substantial reduction of the tariff on the necessaries of life, including foodstuffs, clothing and building materials.
In other words, if I understand the language, expressly and by implication, he means this:	So far as the government
policy applies to reduction of the customs tariff on the primary industries of this country he is content, but he wants them to go just a little bit further in order to give further relief other than the mere incidental relief which will be given to consumers by reason of the government's policy with regard to primary industries. He wants them to give further relief to consumers by reducing the burden of customs taxation. Now that is not any policy that is new; there is nothing new about it. I hold in my hand the policy of the Liberal party; I hold in my hand the policy of the Independent Labour party of Manitoba, upon which my hon. friend was elected; I hold in my hand the new national policy of the Progressive party, and in every one of those platforms adherence is given to the very things which the
hon. gentleman asks for, and some of them, including his own, are almost identical in language with his amendment. That I may say frankly is the policy to which I adhere. It'is the policy upon which 1 was elected; it is the policy which I intend to support.
But it is suggested by other hon. gentlemen that to support the amendment constitutes a vote of want of confidence in the government. Well, I did not know that. It does not constitute a vote of want of confidence in the government unless the government tells us that that is the way they are going to look upon it. But is the government going to call it a vote of want of confidence because some hon. members feel that attention should be directed to further necessary reductions in order that the consumers of this country may get further and larger benefits. This mere fiction, this question of a lack of confidence in the government is something that is inherited from a prehistoric past. Why cannot we get rid of these fictions? Why cannot we eliminate them from our procedure, and to that extent at least be modern and up-to-date? Why not say to the government: We approve of your policy as far as you have gone, and without expressing any lack of confidence in you we think you should investigate and go into these other matters not only of reduction in customs taxation, but also the matter of introducing new: forms of taxation to which you and various other parties in this House are already committed? How can I, elected on a platform containing the principles outlined in the amendment, justify my vote against the amendment by telling my constituents that there is some rule of the House which says that this would mean a vote of want of confidence in the government? I suggest to the Prime Minister, and I do it with all seriousness and in all sincerity, that here would be a splendid opportunity for him to ask the free and unfettered judgment of this House. The question he might direct to the House is this: Are you in favour of a further substantial and immediate reduction of the customs tariff on the articles that are so necessary in the home, and which minister to the shelter, food and comfort of the people? Why cannot he do it? Because of this ridiculous rule to which I refer. Only that and nothing more. This rule, like some other things, should speedily be cast into the limbo of forgotten things, and I suggest to the Prime Minister, here is a time to prove his real democracy and to show that he wants to find the real judgment of the House on this important matter.
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

There are one or two other matters to which I wish to refer. I regret very much that the government the year before last saw fit to introduce an amendment to the Customs Act. I am reading the resolution which was incorporated subsequently into law, in 1922:
If at any time it appears to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council on a report from the Minister of Customs and Excise that natural products of the class or kind produced in Canada are being imported into Canada either on sale or on consignment under such conditions as prejudicially or injuriously to affect the interests of Canadian producers, the Governor in Council may, in any case or class of cases, authorize the minister tc value such goods for duty notwithstanding any of the provisions of this act, and the value so determined shall be held to the fair market value thereof.
I want to give just one illustration of the operation of that provision. In the province of Alberta I regret to say we do not produce as yet any fruit; I am hopeful, however, as to the future, but in the neighbouring province of British Columbia they do produce considerable fruit. Last year fruit was produced in the state of Washington and available for sale on the open market in that state at 80 cents per box. The present customs taxation is 30 cents a box; so disregarding the freight charges the cost to the purchaser in Canada would ordinarily be $1.10 per box for that fruit. But was it that? Not at all. The Minister of Customs, although he could not do it under the Dumping Act, because the Dumping Act takes as its basic figures the fair market value for consumption in the place where produced, under this amendment levied a 15 per cent dumping duty in addition to the duty already imposed, making the cost, disregarding freight, to the consumer $1,261 a box. To that amount must be added, however, the necessary handling charges and the commission agent's charges. What was the result? Simply this: Last year in the province of Alberta the price of apples was so high that the people were denied the opportunity of buying that fruit. What happened? My hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Good) told me last summer that he found them dumping boxes and boxes of apples-I think he said thousands of boxes of apples-in the Okanagan lake somewhere near Vernon. That was the situation-the price was so high that the consumers went on strike, and the whole situation is traceable to this [DOT] nefarious protectionist legislation of 1922. Now, I think the government should do something to relieve that situation. I do not think they should give us freer trade with one hand and take it back with the other. I think the government should take the earliest step to change that legislation so that it will at least 
give the consumers of western Canada opportunity to purchase fruit at reasonable prices
