speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot give the hon. gentleman the information he asks for. I understand the hon. member for Brant proposes to speak later in the debate and he may be in a position to give further details. I am not concerned particularly with the reason for dumping these apples into lake .Okanagan. I can understand from the hon. gentleman's viewpoint that that is a matter of considerable importance, and rightly so. I want to do no injustice, I simply state the fact and I have no doubt the whole of the circumstances will come to light later.
There is another matter to which I personally take very serious objection, and that is the elimination of the exemption clause in the dumping regulations on April 8 last, two days before the budget was introduced. I am not prepared to argue the full effect of that exemption but there can be no doubt it is another step in the direction of protection- it cannot be otherwise. It may be that there is some substantial reason which the government has for this and similar legislation. I

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
mean the similar legislation of 1922. I trust there is some substantial ground for their action. Personally, although I have been anxious to secure information which would justify me in condoning the removal of that exemption legislation, I have not been able to do so.
I want to say in conclusion that many members take the occasion at this time to renew their faith in Canada. I do not think it should be necessary for me to renew my faith in this my native land. I was interested, however, in observing that over one hundred and fifty years ago the habit of expressing faith in the future of this country was then a comparatively common habit. I notice that Dr. Benjamin Franklin, when he was asked by the British Colonial Secretary whether or not it would be a good thing to restore Canada to France, wrote these rather historic words:
I have long been of the opinion that the foundation of the future grandeur and stability of the British Empire lies in America, and though like other foundations they are low and little now, they are nevertheless broad and strong enough to support the greatest political structure that human wisdom has yet erected.
I am therefore by no means for restoring Canada to France.
Again, standing upon the threshold of the twentieth century Sir Wilfrid Laurier, a statesman for whom I hold the highest admiration, expressed his faith in the future of Canada and claimed that the twentieth century belonged to this Dominion. More than one hundred and fifty years have passed since Benjamin Franklin wrote the message to which I referred. A quarter of the century has passed which Sir Wilfrid Laurier claimed for Canada. And yet I would ask any hon. member here if he is impressed with the progress which we have made in the interim. That is the question. Faith is a good thing. Faith is highly desirable, faith is necessary, but faith itself will not avail-faith without works is dead. As a matter of fact our economic future is being welded to-day upon the anvils of continental Europe, and we allow the existing rusty and creaking old legislative machinery to go on quite indifferent to the settlement of our future in those distant countries. The termination of the war brought great hope for reconstruction. Hundreds of thousands of men returned from overseas with a broader outlook and with a new vision for Canada. Thousands here who had been spared contact with Europe also shared in that optimistic outlook. We turned aside from the high opportunity that we had. We deserted the pathway that invited our feet, and we went back as a nation
to the old order and to the old control. These things still persist. That is one reason why 100,000 of those soldiers who offered, for a mere pittance, their services to their country in the time of its peril, accompanied by thousands of others-all denied the security of a livelihood in this country-have sought shelter and asylum in other lands. That is the situation to-day. The plain fact, Mr. Speaker, is that the domestic and international problems of our day lie outside the scope of our present political parties. These problems are economic and geographic in Canada; they do not yield to the same treatment as our problems of fifty years ago. Our forefathers were then disturbed with the questions of political freedom, of the right to vote, and of equality before the law. In that struggle the political parties of to-day undoubtedly took an active and a worthy part, but in the struggle they exhausted themselves and are unable to cope with the new situations arising to-day. As a matter of fact their achievements lie behind us on the battlefields of political freedom. What we need at this time are men and women who will face the problems of to-day.
The main economic problem is now the equitable distribution of the products of industry and, in conjunction with that, to ascertain a common denominator that will weld out of this country, out of its varying and diverse interests, a harmonious whole. That is the problem before the people of Canada to-day. I venture to say that the solutions of these problems will not come from within this parliament. I think perhaps it will come from without parliament from men and women who, with minds receptive to new ideas, who, freed from and unembarrassed by political considerations and affiliations, will bring to the solution of these problems their best, their most earnest and disinterested judgment.
Appropriately enough, Mr. Speaker, for the guidance of all members who enter the portals of this House, is found that old proverb:
Where there is no vision
The people perish.
We are the heirs of a doubtful past. We are the trustees of a challenging future. Shall we as Canadians allow our country to perish for lack of vision? The challenge to-day is to us and to our generation. I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that if we together united seek the salvation of this country we will be able to weld a real nationality, bounded only, like the shield of Achilles, by the blue rim of
ocean.
The Budget*-Mr. Church

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
did not take any part in the debate on the Address, and would not have taken any part in the present debate were it not for the fact that I come from an industrial district which is very much affected by the present financial policy announced in the budget. The district of Toronto has been built up by protection, a great industrial centre having been established there under that great principle. My remarks to-day will deal simply with that great subject of protection, which affects cities and towns in this country; and the financial policy of Canada and the Empire. My remarks to-day will relate to all phases of the problem, the psychology of protection. I support it not because of its own sake but as essential for Canada's sake.
Fortunately we cannot all think or see alike, but while that is so we can respect each other's opinions for what they are worth. We can appreciate the sincerity with which they are held, and give and take, and show moderation and good will. Canada is a difficult country to govern, especially during days like these of stress and strain; and as every government has its troubles, I hope this government will not think that any criticism of the present budget is not made for the good of the country.
Coming from Toronto, I want to express the high regard the people of that city had for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) during his long public career. His unfailing courtesy and kindness won the respect of all members of the House as well as of the people of the country. So far as the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is concerned, I think it but proper to say that he has proved himself to be a most painstaking and obliging minister, and deserves a great deal of credit for the manner in which he has performed his duties since taking over the department.
I had intended placing before the House a number of letters in regard to the very serious injury done to Toronto's industries by the instability of tariff, the doubt, uncertainty and unrest resultant industrially from the lack of stability and the tinkering with the tariff. Similar letters to these were read by the member for West Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) and therefore I shall not take time to read them as he has fully covered the ground of the damage done to industries.
If Canada is to have free trade or semifree trade, why are we spending such a huge sum of money on the Wembley Exhibition? When the Prince of Wales, as president, attended the opening of the exhibition at

Wembley he made a speech in addressing the King from which I quote the following:
I hope, Sir, that the result of this exhibition will be to impress vividly upon all the peoples of your Empire the advice you have given to them on more than one occasions, that they should be fully awake to their responsibilities as heirs of so glorious a heritage and that they should be in nowise slothful stewards, but that they should work unitedly and energetically to develop the resources of the Empire for the benefit of the British race, for the benefit of those other races which have accepted our guardianship over their destinies, and for the benefit of mankind generally.
I may say that the free traders of Manchester and the Northwest Free Trade Union have, under government auspices in England, been endeavouring to turn the British Empire Exhibition into a free trade affair and they have secured space for their free trade exhibit. The Wembley exhibition was designed to help forward the cause of Imperial trade, to show the wealth and completeness of the natural resources of the British Empire and the enormous possibilities of development represented in Imperial trade, and it might, I think, have been left free of the efforts to capture it.
The Progressives in this House, not to be outdone by their friends in England, might seek to exhibit their free trade wares at Wembley by asking the government to give them over part of the Canadian space at the exhibition. As the member for Brome tMr. McMaster) and the Progressives practically believe that the whole future of Canada depends on free trade, I hope that such an exhibit, if made, will be thorough and that it will at least present a candid and truthful view of our economic situation. I venture in all modesty to suggest to the Progressives and Liberals some suitable models and diagrams for this suggested Canadian exhibit at Wembley: A model of the vigorous enforcement of the Combines Act and trusts by the Minister of Labour: a portrait of the hon. member for Brome, with a shadow of his riding being wiped out by the Redistribution Act, crossing back again to the government side and of the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Marler) exchanging places with the member for Brome on the cross benches; a painting in oils of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), tolling the church union bell, announcing to the world the death knell of protection in Canada. As there is such a stiff economy contest for branch lines, Hudson bay canals, towers and breakwaters, I suggest that the Progressives include an oil painting of all these works. The unused timber and planks in-the Liberal platforms of 1896, 1911 and 1919 might also

The Budget-Mr. Church
be used. The shattered planks of the United Farmers of Ontario might be included; also an exhibit of the Progressives branch line economy planks, to be built only according to the free trade law of supply and demand.
A further section of the exhibit might show how the Progressives are aiding the exodus to the United States by their free trade fallacies. A section might be devoted to the roadbuilding methods of the United Farmers of Ontario under the Hon. Mr. Biggs and their way of handling bonds and loans in Ontario, under the so-called group system in that province, with a portrayal of the leader of the Progressives (Mr.. Forke) assuring the government before the session that they would have his support. Further, there might be a tintype of three prominent government members talking one way and then voting another way on the tariff. There might also be a miniature of the Progressives ceasing to be the "dilapidated annex," and becoming an overflow, and "the spare men" on the government team, with the leader o.f the Progressives the star pinch hitter on the government team whenever called into play. They might begin by having the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master),-who is so fond of free trade and the dead text books of the past, which he quoted the other night while dealing with free trade-and ask him to quote the frenzied prophecies of Cobden and Bright that the whole world would follow England's example of free trade. They might also show the fulfilment of that prophecy in the rising tariff . walls of every country but our own. They might show the comparative positions of British, German, French and American industries, when free trade was adopted by England and protection by the other three countries I have named. Then Germany was the poorest country in Europe, content, or forced to export such raw products as corn and timber in exchange for the manufactures of industrial England. They might show the Prussian peasant of that time, as contemporary travellers describe him, dressed in rags, breaking the clods with a wooden mallet because he was too poor to buy an iron plough. They might also quote the pathetic and almost despairing description of the German economist List, who described England about 1840 as:
Supreme in every branch of manufacture,
Contrary to what the hon. member for Brome said the other night.
-as a world's metropolis which supplies all nations with manufactured goods, a treasure house of all great capital, a banking establishment for all nations, which controls the circulating medium of the whole world, and by loans and the receipt of interest on them
makes all the peoples of the earth her tributaries.
In vain,-
List added.
-did the Germans humble themselves to the position of hewers of wood and drawers of water to the Britons; the latter treated them worse than a subject people.
Then we should see the United States at that same time, in 1840, almost wholly an agricultural country invaded every year by an army of British commercial travellers. We should then have a picture of a comparative situation of the three countries at the outbreak of the war, Germany producing twice as much steel and iron as England, the United States with an even vaster production, the two countries towering in their industrial strength above the nation which had ouce supplied both with everything they required except food and timber. These comparative diagrams might be accompanied by others to show how national power was a reflection of industrial power, and how free trade England which, as a protected country, had once ruled the world, was compelled to invoke the aid of one great protected country, the United States, to assist her in repelling the attack of another.
There are endless possibilities for this free trade exhibit. We might have a very pretty model of England in 1840 as the workshop of the world, and another in 1924, under free trade as described the other day by the hon. member for Brome and this afternoon by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson), as the workhouse of the world with a dole system as the fountain. We might have a beautiful and moving reproduction of a labour exchange, for the benefit of the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine), with the clerk handing out, not work, but doles to a queue of about a million and a quarter people. We might have exhibits of crumbling factories, rusting machinery and cold furnaces. The National Union of Manchester could contribute some very interesting statistics, the result of a questionnaire which they sent recently to their members. It seems that 567 manufacturers who replied, estimated that with adequate protection they alone could employ over 100.000 extra hands. But the most interesting exhibits of all would be a list of the' German and other foreign members of the Cobden Club and the German cheques which have come in to assist the free trade cause in England. Do we want to head for such a state of affairs in Canada? Then you have only to adopt the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture and you will have in Canada such a state of affairs as I have described as existing in the Mother Country to-day under free trade.
The Budget-Mr. Church

In speaking of the subject of protection I wish to refer for a moment or two to the psychology of protection as applied to this country. Great Britain, France, Germany, Russia and the United States have all been built .up and their manufactures developed and maintained by protection in every method and manner possible which the legislatures could devise, those methods varying down the ages, although there have been free trade lapses. After great wars through the centuries between these great powers protection was brought up to date to meet changed conditions. For , many centuries protection to native industries was the leading policy of all the states foremost in industry and commerce-protection to home industries on land as well as shipping and that protection enforced on both land and sea. Under such high protection, established and made adequate to foster native industries, the great basic manufactures of these states were developed and sustained. Chronic free traders will tell you that they were established and developed in spite of protection. Not so. They give us no table of facts to substantiate their argument. England is no example of free trade. In England, 1,500,000 to 2,000,000 men are out of work under free trade and a man cannot get a job there because of free trade.
Ill fares the land to hastening ills a prey,
Where free trade flourishes and men decay.
Rural depopulation is acute also. A man cannot get a job in Canada because for practically all intents and purposes we have semifree trade in this country, and the situation will become more acute under the low tariff before us. Nearly 200,000 people have swelled the exodus to the United States during the past fiscal year, and that exodus will be greater than ever under this new tariff with five cents off here and ten cents off there, and with nobody able to say where the end will be. Under this condition of affairs the industries of the city from which I . come are very much disturbed and the unrest is becoming more acute. This instability of tariff is going to paralyze business, make it stagnant and cause hard times. England, as I say, is no example of free trade, because her manufactures for centuries had been developed beyond those of other nations under protection long before the adoption of free trade there. England was built up under a rigid system of protection, protection not only by a tariff, but by navigation laws and many other agencies which her legislature during those 200 years could develop and put into force. In economic questions, this country will be guided by facts, by experience and by actual conditions as to free trade and protection and not

by any abstract theory of any theoretical school of thought, as propounded the other evening by the hon. member for Brome in quoting John Stuart Mill and John Bright.
Mr. John Bright made many prophecies and lived to see most of them falsified. In his speech at the Cobden celebration in 1877 he saw this vision:	[DOT]
If we look into France we see that protection is becoming weaker.
Is that true to-day? Why, Sir, you have only to look at the high wall of protection which France has erected since the war.
If' we look at the United States or consult any intelligent American we shall find that there it is shaken and tottering to its fall.
Nearly fifty years have passed and protection, in all the great countries of Europe and America, has a firmer hold on the public mind now than then; and during sixty-eight years since the repeal of the Com Laws public opinion in all the great commercial and manufacturing countries has gradually settled down more and more in favour of protection.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
food zones, the thrift of its people, its invigorating and salubrious climate all point to Canada as bound to become the great industrial country of America.
The tariff should be taken out of politics. It is rot a political question in any sense. Authorities should be set up in this country to act in an advisory capacity to the government in relation to this problem. I would not advocate the appointment of another tariff commission, because commissions have not been a success in this country. The Railway Commission for instance, does it regulate railways? No. sometimes it gets lost, strajmd or stolen. You have a grain commission, does it regulate matters respecting grain? 1 trow not. The government of the day should be responsible for the tariff. The Minister of Finance is the minister responsible with respect to tariff matters, and I would suggest that instead of appointing a tariff commission, a rate expert with a staff should be appointed under the control of the minister, T.o figure out the fair price ratio of tariff for agricultural implements and everything else that belongs to the manufactures and' after allowing for overhead and other costs he should fix a price, and that price should be stabilized and standardized. In that way you would have all the advantages of a tariff commission without its defects.
The Liberal-Conservative party have always been protectionist from Sir John A. Macdonald down to to-day. In the last general election our very able and capable leader the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) preached this same doctrine of adequate protection for the industries of this country, down in the Maritime provinces, in central Canada, and out in the West. There was no beating about the bush with him. Everyone knew where he stood on the tariff, and that has always been the policy of the Conservative party. They have always stood for moderate protection-adequate protection for the industries of this country.
After all, it was not any political party that made Canada a nation. The people themselves had something to do with making this Dominion a nation, but in my opinion it was the National Policy that made Canada the country it is to-day. You may criticise the National Policy as you like, you may criticise the principle of protection, but we never had anything else but protection in this country except for a brief period so far as I know. I have placed the tariffs of the respective governments in Canada in

parallel columns and compared them; and I doubt whether anybody could call the tariff that has been in operation from 1896 down until the present budget anything but a protective tariff. I think that any economic writer would certainly consider that the tariffs for which my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is responsible were all highly protective.
Eighty-five per cent of the crops produced in the province of Ontario have a home market in the near-by cities and towns, at the highest price that can be got in open competition in the world to-day. That home market is a steady market; it is not one that is here to-day and away to-morrow. It is to be found in the cities and towns that surround the many very fine agricultural counties of Ontario. I do not think the farmers there believe in free trade. If it were not for protection, in view of the hostile tariff in the United States these farmers would be one hundred per cent worse off than they are to-day, and I believe that remark applies to eastern Canada generally.
The late Hon. J. Israel Tarte once said that platforms were made to get in on, but not to stand on. Probably that accounts for the Liberals from 1896 to 1911 not carrying out their free trade policies, but returning and sticking to protection. I do not blame them for it. Any prosperity that this country had during that period was due to protection. All the main cities and towns of Canada have been built up under protection. That is true of Brantford, of Toronto, of Hamilton, of Montreal and all our other large cities. They have all been built up by the National Policy. Take the city of Toronto, which I represent. In 1878 soup kitchens had to be established there to meet the wants of the large number of men who were out of employment; vacant houses and stores were many; and there were evidences of distress on every hand. But the policy of protection was adopted and it stimulated the growth of our city in many ways. The trade and commerce of Toronto greatly increased; the population has doubled almost every ten years; the receipts from customs and excise, and post office, to say nothing of bank clearings grew prodigiously, and Toronto is only one of the many cities of Canada that has made tremendous strides as the result of protection. Now, geography has taught the people of Canada a lesson in more ways than one. It has taught them not to leave themselves at the mercy of a foreign country in regard to their fiscal affairs, especially when that country is one

The Budget-Mr. Church
of the most wealthy, powerful, prosperous and ambitious in the world-I refer to the United States. Every country in the world including the United States, is increasing its tariff. Not only are the United States and the various countries in Europe doing that, but Australia, New Zealand, and the South American republics are all adding to their protective tariffs. Is it to be argued that these countries are all wrong, and that the Progressives and Liberals of Canada are all right? I say no. I maintain that as a result of the Great War and of world industrial conditions, more protection will be required to meet the changing conditions that arise as the years go by.
I once heard Sir Richard Cartwright and Sir Oliver Mowat say that if the Liberals were returned to office in 1896 they would remove the last vestige of protection, but they did not	do
so. Examine the sixteen budgets of the present Minister of Finance and what do we find? We find that each and every one is highly protective in character. But that cannot be said of the budget we are now considering. I do not see what the Canadian farmer is going to do. He is shut out of the United States by a tariff of 42 cents a bushel on his wheat and therefore must depend on his home market. That is the best market for him that I know of. It will take care of from 80 to 85 per cent of his crop in the central part of Canada. If the government can solve the railway problem and bring the railway rates down, a great step will have been taken. A great deal of disturbance and harm has been wrought in the city from which I come by the present budget. Very few people realize what a large proportion of the population of such cities as Toronto, Hamilton, Brantford, and the towns of an industrial character surrounding them are dependent for livelihood upon our basic industries. There are merchants, clerks, tailors, dressmakers, milliners, doctors, lawyers, school teachers, carpenters, bricklayers, plasterers, painters, decorators, plumbers, electricians, real estate agents, insurance agents and many others who get their living by supplying the varied wants of the industrial population. All these people contribute in a variety of ways to the general revenues of the government. If they were living in the United States instead of Canada they would contribute nothing to Canadian government revenue. The loss of revenue resulting from even the partial wiping out of the agricultural implement industry would greatly
exceed the amount required to pay the freight charges on agricultural implements from the factory to the farm.
In a new country like Canada essentially agricultural, one of the chief wants has been markets. Now food markets at home mean better prices and better profits and better wages. They stimulate production and lead to wealth. If we all produced the same articles there would be no market. It was because British farmers had their customers, the British manufacturers, almost at their doors, and that many corn producing countries had no manufacturers that Britain became so prosperous. It is as true to-day as it was in Adam Smith's day when he said that "the increase and riches of commercial and manufacturing towns contribute to the improvement and cultivation of the countries to which they belong in many ways by affording a great and ready market for the rude produce of the country." We must have home markets for a hundred products of the farm and garden and the fields that are too bulky or perishable to bear transit to other countries. Under the present tariff we are heading for the same conditions that prevailed in 1878-for depression, closed industries and hard times.
The present budget is injudicious and not judicious protection. By "judicious protection" I mean protection brought up to date to meet the varied conditions created by the war and conditions at home and abroad- a protection which will promote and maintain on a living basis our own domestic industries in this land of abundant resources. It must be such a tariff as will conserve and strengthen our existing industries, further develop them, and nurse other struggling ones and those needing aid, such a policy as would call into existence other new industries and assist in maintaining them after they are created; such a tariff as would in effect stop the present exodus to the United States by creating profitable employment which would accumulate * wealth and minimize the waste now going on in the country and check the economic wastage of the present exodus. The greatest problem confronting this parliament is to adopt such a national policy as I suggest here brought up to date as will bring "the field and factory" together; will preserve our own home markets for our own resources and products; will eliminate all unnecessary hauling to and fro and cheapen production and make it more accessible to the masses rather than develop a system which elevates trade above production.
The Budget-Mr. Church

As has been said Cobdenism has the defect of considering the exchange of commodities as being more important than their production. The aim of protection as we had it in Canada under the Conservatives was to promote production and avoid waste-the only economic policy that will ever endure in Canada. How will the so-called reductions benefit those out of work? Will not the departure from last year's declaration of the Minister of Finance for stability of tariffs ead to a wobbling and meddling tariff policy, and add to the number of industries closed down with attendant unrest, uneasiness and unemployment. Will there not be a further economic waste by way of further exodus to the United States if we keep on nibbling at our tariff and lowering the same? Will we not lose' what industrial supremacy we have? At present Chicago is the "third largest Canadian city in the world" and Detroit is the fourth. I use these designations to illustrate the number of Canadians now living in these two cities of the United States. Where will this exodus stop under "a vaster free trade policy than has been "? Little Effect Felt in Canada From New U.S. Tariff on Wheat
Exports Became Greater as Date of Increase Drew . Near-American Officials Look for Bigger Volume in This Class of Business.
Ottawa, April 14.-The new United States tariff of forty-two cents per bushel on wheat went into effect last week, but it had no effect here nor in any other part of the country, as far as officials can learn. As the date for the incoming of the increase drew near exports of wheat to the Republic increased, chiefly of that intended for milling in bond for export purposes.
The information here is that American federal trade officials consider that a considerable increase in this class of business is to be expected. If the American mills cannot get at a reasonable price Canadian wheat for mixing for flour for home they will get more to mill in bond for export. As a matter of fact, during the last month the number of bonded United States mills grinding Canadian hard wheat for export has increased from two to six.
Many Americans who follow the milling industry closely are of the opinion that one of the effects of this higher duty on wheat will be to make Buffalo, rather than Minneapolis, the centre of the hard wheat grinding in bond for export business. Further evidence of the tendency for this form of industry to locate in Buffalo is to be seen in the additional fact that the well-known Palisade mill at Minneapolis is being taken down and transferred to Buffalo.

The total cost of the Toronto viaduct to this parliament would amount to about $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 spread over three or four years, or the cost of one or two branch lines. Our free (trade friends have great 
confidence in the law of supply and demand, and we shall be satisfied if they will apply the same principle in the case of the Toronto viaduct; for I can assure this House that if the work in connection with the viaduct is carried to a completion it will more than justify the expenditure which this parliament may vote towards it. With the increased volume of business which would follow, both in freight and in passenger traffic, the viaduct would pay for itself.
Coming now to the post office, some questions have been asked about the receipts in the city of Toronto. In this regard, it will interest the House to know that the receipts of the post office in Toronto are equal to those of many cities put together, having amounted last year to the sum of $5,798,000. This year it will exceed $6,000,000, and notwithstanding this fact the city of Toronto cannot get decent post office accommodation. It has to put up with a lot of ramshackle buildings in which its business men finS it extremely inconvenient to do business. In this connection, I must express my disappointment at the fact that the budget has not disclosed a return to the two cent postal rate. This reduction would in my opinion be a step in the right direction, because nothing retards trade and commerce so much as high postal rates.
So far as the sales tax is concerned, it seems to me that the ingenuity of a Philadelphia lawyer is required to work out the government's scheme, which strikes one as a makeshift affair. The impression that one gets is that we have a landed aristocracy and a retail aristocracy in Canada. The tax in its new form is on the basis of robbing Peter to pay Paul-one figure being taxed one class and another figure another class of the population. I believe that the city of Toronto pays between $8,000,000 and $9,000,000 of this tax, although it is difficult to get at the returns, that city being linked up with other places.
In regard to the Canadian National Exhibition, I may say that the taxpayers of Toronto have spent between $13,000,000 and $14,000,000 on grounds of permanent buildings, permanent exhibits, and so forth; and during the war the exhibition was continued, thus keeping up the morale of the people. How much has this parliament contributed towards the maintenance of that institution? In 1920 parliament voted $5,000 but in 1921 the grant was disallowed, and since then the Dominion has given nothing; it has not even offered what one might call pin money to this highly deserving national institution. The taxpayers of Toronto, I would add, have

also paid out of their pockets nearly $2,000,000 for the purpose of carrying on the educational work of the Department of Agriculture, having spent this money on the erection of a Coliseum for the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair. But out of this expenditure the city has got nothing, although other parts of the country have profited thereby.
I hope that this year something will be done to improve present conditions in regard to the income tax. The United States are doing something for the working classes in that country in this connection, and I am personally absolutely opposed to any doubleheader tax; I do not believe that people should be called upon to pay an income tax to the Dominion in addition to what they pay to the city. On May 1, the income tax will be payable to the Dominion and on May 9 to the city of Toronto, and this double [DOT] tax reacts on all the working classes of the city. In my opinion no one should be called upon to pay a federal income tax on an income below six or seven thousand dollars; and as a matter of fact I do not know whether it is just constitutional to compel people to pay that tax to the Dominion at all. To my mind, it is just a question whether this parliament has power to impose an income tax upon the people except for war purposes or for the purposes generally of militia and national defence. And the war having concluded years ago, I think the time has come when we should do away with that tax because it bears heavily on small wage earners in the cities and towns. Even the poor school teacher has an income tax to pay as well as those who are in better financial circumstances than himself.
With regard to the subject of public health, I want to say a word in approval of the policy of President Coolidge, who has appointed a commission to look into the question of public recreation and to formulate a programme in this connection. A few years ago we had no public health department in this country, but such a department having been established is now doing good work, and I would commend to the attention of the government what President Coolidge has done in regard to outdoor recreation for the people. No doubt some responsible minister of the Crown could take this matter up and do something for the good of the people.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with very much interest to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) I am sure his account of the trials of Toronto tax-payers affected the House quite visibly, and, with others, I wept at his recital. I have to say that the constituency which I represent is probably more affected by the changes in the tariff than any other constituency in the country, and therefore it may seem appropriate that, although the hour is late, I should say a few words upon the motion and the amendment before the House.
I was trudging along the government highway contentedly when I came to a fork in the road-not necessarily spelt with an "e" Mr. Speaker-and surveyed the path. I thought I would keep to the right hand road, for that to the left seemed to lead down to a land of swamp and muskeg, of sloughs and quagmires, where parties were chasing that ignis fatuus, that will-o'-the-wisp,-free trade. It has been said that imitation is the sincerest flattery, Mr. Speaker, so I will endeavour to follow the very good example set by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), in his speech, which was a model of brevity and conciseness, and explain in as few words as possible my position upon this question.
In the budget presented by the Acting Minister of Finance there is, of course, a great deal that must be a source of congratulation to everyone in the country; there is no denying it. For the first time for many years the account has been settled on the right side of our national ledger; we have been able now to produce a surplus that will go toward reducing the national debt, and I look upon it as the turning of an important corner in the country's financial history.
Taking off the sales tax on many articles entirely and reducing it on some others is something for which also we must add a word of congratulation to the minister.
As to what he said about the condition of our national railways, I have always regarded the system as one of the most important to this country. It is a system that we should all watch with the greatest interest, for it is not only the greatest railway system in the world, it is Canada's greatest national asset, and upon it depends all our avenues of wealth, of commerce and of industry, all our basic industries, and every other industry. The progress that has been made by our national railways in the last year and a half in efficiency, in the service they render, and in the improvement of their financial position, is phenomenal. From the time when the president, Sir Henry Thornton, was appointed,

is not much more than a year and a half ago, and what has been accomplished in that time is extraordinary and is something that should be a source of hearty congratulation to every Canadian who takes an interest in his country and feels the importance of this great national asset.
One matter that I should like to have seen touched upon in the budget-I have mentioned it before-because I think it is one of the forms of taxation which touch everybody, and perhaps the general population almost equally, is the war stamp on letters. I should like it to have been possible for the Acting Minister of Finance to remove this tax. We are almost the only country, I believe, that retains it. I hope the time will come in the not far distant future when the general taxation of the country will be reduced by the removal of the war stamp on letters. It would be a boon not only to business men but to correspondents all over the country and would do away with the anomaly that I pointed out last year, namely, that letters can be sent cheaper to Mexico and the United States than to the Old Country and many of our British possessions.
These are matters of congratulation; but when it comes to changes in the tariff I cannot congratulate the minister, I cannot say that they quite meet with my approval in the same way, and I shall endeavour to show the reasons why, and in doing so to point out that those reasons are applicable not only to Brantford, the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and to the province of Ontario generally, but to the whole Dominion. A great American, Bayard Taylor, said, that as no two human beings observed any object by the same ray of light, it could not appear exactly the same to any two of them; and it seems to me that I observe these tariff changes from a different point of view to that of any other member. Therefore I shall endeavour to justify my attitude, and if it seems to you, Sir, that I am ploughing a lonely furrow, I assure you I shall endeavour to do so with a Brantford plough.
I may say that duties on agricultural implements have a kind of history which, if you will bear with me, I will briefly relate. I believe in the time which has been so often referred to by gentlemen opposite, when the National Policy was introduced, the duty on agricultural implements was not less than 35 per cent. That duty was from time to time reduced,-indeed on an agricultural necessity of production, binder twine, it was removed altogether, and the article made free. Wtehad then two factories in Brantford, and there were

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
some 24 throughout the Dominion; to-day we have one factory in Brantford and there are two others in Canada, the other 21 having vanished. Now, when the duty on agricultural implements was reduced in 1919 it was 22i per cent on ploughs and 174 per cent on binders. An additional 5 per cent was taken off in that year. The duty on binders was reduced to 124 per cent, and on ploughs to 174 per cent. Representations were, of course, made in this House. At the same time farm tractors below a value of some $1,400 or $1,500 were made free. The result was that in the next two years $20,000,000 of farm tractors were imported, and the two farm tractor industries in Brantford went out of that line of business entirely. That so much affected the industry in Brantford, and the feeling of the people in Brantford at that time-I am speaking of five years ago-was such that the representative of Brantford then found it necessary to vote against the adoption of the budget of. his own party, because he was a loyal Conservative and it was brought down by a Conservative government. He voted against that budget protesting against the reduction of the duties on this industry, because it seemed as though the agricultural implement industry had been singled out for reduction ahead of all other industries.
Two years ago, in 1922, a still further reduction was made of 2i per cent on ploughs and 2i per cent on binders, reapers and mowers, reducing the duty on ploughs to 15 per cent, and on harvesting machinery to 10 per cent. At the time of the general election when I became a candidate in 1921, we had felt these various reductions in the duties on our principal industries, because as you are aware the agricultural implement industry is the principal industry of Brantford. The present duties will affect some seven or eight of our largest factories in Brantford, and at the time of that election the question of the duty was, of course, a very, very ddicate one, and it was felt that it was not in the interest of the city, and not in the interest of the workmen in the industry and those who had their homes there, nor in the interest of the factories, that the duty should be still further reduced, and when I became a candidate at that time a part of my platform was that I would oppose any further reduction in the duties on the industries of Brantford, any duties that would act in a way that would be inimical to the best interests of the factories or industries of Brantford. I did not think at that time that I would be called upon in the first year I came into this House, that was two years
ago, to see a still further reduction of 21 per cent, which, as you will remember, was made; but that having been made, it seemed to me that we had reached the irreducible minimum on agricultural implements. The duties were then lower than on any other articles of manufacture that were made in Canada, and I thought, and it was the opinion generally of the people of the city and of those engaged in the industry, that having reached that point it should be considered the irreducible minimum, and that no steps should be taken below that to give American competitors the advantage of obtaining access to our market. Now when that is the case, I think that every member of this House will see that my duty is clear as far as this budget is concerned, with reference to those resolutions that still further reduce the duty on agricultural implements.

Why not take the duty off locomotives, off railway cars, off the thousand and one other things that 'are used on a railway and not simply off ploughs. Hon. members opposite have said several times that they believe in justice and in a square equal deal for all, and special privileges for none. The feeling of a man who is working in an industry where his product, we will say, is sold in an unprotected market has been expressed many times by the hon. members of the Progressive party. They

When the tariff is mentioned we are taken away back into the past and treated pretty much to the same discourse on Cobden and Bright. But this year we were taken back even as far as Walpole and Pitt. Very well. I do not know the exact circumstance that caused him to bring it in, but I presume that when he introduced the great philosopher's name he expected it would have some weight with us. I could not say what weight it could have in Canada, which he did not know, and on a business question when he knew nothing whatever of business. His principles were so peculiar and so erratic it seems to me he would hardly be considered an authority even on an economic question when that question is to be decided in Canada.
But with regard to John Stuart Mill, if the hon. member wishes to pay attention to that great philosopher I would respectfully refer him to his work on logic, his unrivalled work on logic. If he refers to that work he will find in it many times cautions against misstating a coincidence for a consequence; that one of the fatal mistakes in logic is to mistake a coincidence for a consequence. And when the hon. member tells us that in Britain, along in the times he mentions and close to the "hungry forties," trade began to grow and expand and increase by leaps and bounds-when he attributes that to free trade he will find if he looks a little more accurately into it that while it was a coincidence it was not by any means a consequence. Because there were authorities in that day who said that that wonderful progress came from what has been called "the industrial revolution"; that it came from the fact that English inventors in the textile industries, in the engineering industries, in the shipbuilding industry, and in others, made wonderful advances; that steam was applied to technical use and used in all her factories-used in all her factories to such an extent that writing at the moment Emerson said, "Steam may be called an Englishman," and that has been said by some to be the cause of the wonderful progress and advancement that was made in her commerce. It was also the time of Britain's colonial expansion, it was the time when Australia was settled, when business was opened up with India. These are some of the reasons given for the commercial advancement of that time. So I say it is impossible to prove that it was a consequence of free trade, although it was a coincidence. And when gentlemen say, as they have said in this House, that the United States has progressed and got -wealthy in spite of and not because of protection it seems to me that we may take that just in the same way. I do not think the tariff has made or marred either of these two countries. I do not think it has been the one essential that made

the United States have a protective tariff, nor do I think it was free trade that made England so happy and prosperous as she was.
But these gentlemen talk of the wonderful attainments in England at that time, and the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) read a very delightful- editorial from the Journal, I think it was, on "Hats off to Britain." It was a most delightful article and I was very glad to hear my hon. friend read it, I quite enjoyed it. Why, the British tariff or the American tariff is only an incident. It is not a cause of a nation's success or failure; a tariff is a tax. I maintain that the quality that these gentlemen lost sight of is the predominant quality in the British character-it is their love of justice. They would not support a tariff that stripped the protection off one set of industries and left others enjoying it. It was that quality of justice that led to all the great advances in that country, not perhaps commercial or financial; but it was the quality of justice that made them remove the disabilities on Roman Catholics. It was the quality of justice that made them enlarge the franchise in the Reform Bill of 1832. It was the quality of justice that made them in 1833 free the slaves and pay the bill out of their own pocket. The quality of justice should never be forgotten, and what I complain of in the treatment of Brantford in reference to agricultural implements is that I do not think that quality has been observed. Brantford seems to have been always made the goat for all the experiments in the treatment or reduction of the tariff, more than any other manufacturing city in Canada.	,

I do not think it is strange that that should seem mortifying to the people engaged in these industries.
People have said, and hon. members have sometimes said, "Oh, they pay no duty in the United States; why don't your implement factories export implements to that country?" Some of the goods we send over there-and I say this without fear of successful contradiction-are sent over simply because they are absolutely unrivalled by any of the manufactures in the United States. With that exception, it is impossible for us to send much over to the United States, and why? The amendment is quite contrary to the policy of the Labour party in Canada, as expressed at page 55 of this book which I hold in my hand, which is the report of the convention of the great Trades and Labour Council, the chief arm of labour in the whole country. This is the annual report of the convention held in Winnipeg in 1921. Hon. members would think that when this labour convention was held in his own constituency, the leader of that party would be heard from, but his name is not. in the book from one cover to the other. And why not? Because by the Trades and Labour Council of Canada he is not recognized as a leader or labour representative, and yet he stands in this House as a representative of labour, and as a representative of labour introduces that amendment. I want to say on behalf of the labour people of Brantford, and on behalf of the great industrial centre I represent, that the sentiments of the Labour party are not contained in his amendment at 113i
all but are quite contrary to it; and that the expressed opinion of the Trades and Labour Council, as set forth in one of the articles, is that they believe that a tariff should be maintained for the protection of Canadian workmen against competition from outside the country, and that no change should be made in that tariff until a tariff board has been established and the matter looked into with the greatest care. Now in order that we may be exact, I have here a letter from the secretary of the Trades and Labour Council of Brantford enclosing a resolution dated 7th March, which reads :
Moved by Del. Sevigny and seconded by Del. James:
Be it resolved that in the opinion of the Trades and Labour Council of the city of Brantford the most satisfactory solution of the recurring tariff controversies, which have raised so much political confusion and instability in matters of trades and commerce, and thus of serious concern of the workers employed in industry, is to be found in the very clear and decisive declaration, repeatedly adopted by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada in annual convention an extract of which appears in the annual reports of the Hamilton convention of 1919. the Windsor convention of 1920, the Winnipeg convention of 1921, and the Vancouver convention of 1923. Said extract reads as follows:
"During past years there has been carried on a very active campaign by certain interests for the adoption of a free trade policy in Canada. To the numbers of workers engaged by Canadian branches of United States industries, and other industries claiming tariff protection as necessary for their existence, this question is a vital one. Your executive are of the opinion that tariff decisions should cease to be made a matter of political expediency and the decision for their maintenance or abolition, should be reached only after exhaustive inquiry and with a view to enabling the worker, in such industries to be paid proper wage standards without destroying the industry by unfair competition from industries outside of Canada. We recommend the formation of a tariff board, on which organized labor should have proper representation, created with full powers to deal with this subject in a similar manner to the powers exercised by the Railway Commission on railway matters."
This resolution was unanimously adopted.
Yours very truly,
The Brantford Trades and Labour Council C. L. Sevigny.

The third letter that I have here is apparently an answer to some communication that they have had with the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). In it they do not appear to have quite agreed in the course of their communications with one another, but they state that at the last provincial election in Ontario the Independent Labour party, which, I believe, is the one represented by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg, were not able to elect a single man, although they ran candidates in all the chief industrial centres of Ontario. It goes on to say that the party was so far disorganized by this that they did not hold their annual convention on Good Friday as they should have done. That was apparently, the writer says, the end of the party, and they even asked for no flowers at the funeral. I say then that, in order that the stand of the workmen of Ontario shall be rightly understood, this position should be rightly understood. They are not in favour of that amendment; they do not want it, and *if there is that sympathy between labour as the Progressives have claimed from time to time in this House, they should vote against this resolution as every representative of the Trades and Labour party in Brantford would vote against it. I maintain-and I do so with respect-that the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg stands in a false position in this House when he pretends to represent the Labour party of that part of Canada from which I come, and I know whereof I speak. Therefore, from what I have said, hon. members will imagine that I cannot vote for the amendment.
In conclusion, let me say just this, that I think the true aim and policy of all people in this country is to arrive at some kind of a

policy on which we can be agreed. It is certain that if we follow in one direction so that certain parts of the country are under a free trade system, then, in equity and in justice, the whole country will have to go on with that system. I am aware that at the present time efforts have been made by the manufacturers to make representations to the government that if certain concessions were made on their raw material, that would help them to stand the cut in the duty, and I believe the government have done what they can to meet this. But in spite of that, I think and I maintain now seriously that the duty as it existed should be considered as an irreducible minimum upon agricultural implements. I think we should endeavour to establish a board of tariff reference, as the Labour party have asked for-and it has been part of their platform for years- a board which, of course, we understand, could not have any legislative power, which could not impose or take off tariffs, but which could obtain from an independent source whatever information was required by the government of the day and place before it that information in order that it might make for the country the most scientific tariff possible.
1 am not going to be drawn into the old argument of free trade and protection, because I do not think free trade is sensible or practical. It is a mere theory; it is something that does not exist. I do not believe, ff the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) were Minister of Finance, he would go any nearer free trade probably than the present budget, in spite of all his protestations. There are certain things that exist in,theory and that, in theory, are very nice, but in practice are utterly impossible. One of them is universal peace. Who would find fault with the man who advocated universal peace and loved the idea, and yet what word was more hated during the war than the word "pacifist"? It was hated just as much as the word "traitor", because when the country was fighting for its very life, vre knew that the pacifist was almost as much an obstruction to our success as the traitor.
Another thing that great professors and minds have sought after is perpetual motion. No sane man ever started after perpetual motion and remained sane very long. No man ever attained perpetual motion, unless, perhaps, the hon. member for North Toronto. (Mr. Church). I mean to say that no man ever followed the pursuit of that subject and retained his sanity. I am rapidly coming to the conclusion that the question of the-

oretical free trade is very much the same. When I listen to those men who follow it and who rise and discourse here eloquently upon free trade and its advantages, I often think of what has become of that other will-o'-the-wisp, perpetual motion, and those who have pursued it, many of whom you will find in lunatic asylums. I hope that will never be the case of those men who advocate that financial and fiscal policy for our country.
What we want is a policy that will build up the industries of the country, that will tend to the development of its resources, that will bring from northern Ontario those vast treasures that were so eloquently described by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) in his admirable speech. What we want too. is a tariff policy that will protect labour in this country, that wall protect the labouring man, and as labour is added to every article from the raw material to the finished articles, let there be enough protection on that man in the way of a tariff that his industry may be protected. In that wTay we can in time develop this country so that the raw material that we are now exporting to other countries and that they are making money on by manufacturing, we shall be able to manufacture in this country. I do not advocate a policy of exclusion; I do not say that we can be absolutely self-contained. But Canada should export manufactured goods instead of raw material, allowing somebody else to export the manufactured goods, because we know that the one who exports the manufactured goods makes by far the larger profit.
Why can we not export the manufactured goods?	.

I say: Why can we not? Those that we have to export we can and do export; but when it comes to the raw material, the hon. member might have heard the hon. member for North Toronto a few minutes ago instance asbestos down in Quebec, how that was dug out of the bowels of the friendly earth, how we sent it to the United States where some $9,000,000 worth was turned into a value of $60,000,000.

Why do we send it to the
United States?

Because we have no
factories here to manufacture it. We want to develop those factories, those industries. If we do not do that, we shall never be able to export the manufactured article, because they have the factories in the United States
and we shall have to send the raw material to their factories to be manufactured. The difference between the American tariff which gives them protection and ours was rather hidden by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) this afternoon, when he said that they collect in duties $450,000,000 and we collect 8105,000,000. W'hat is the truth about the American tariff? If hon. members examine it for themselves, they will find that articles that the Americans want in free they allow to come in free; but as regards those articles which they do not want, you cannot climb over their tariff wall. Their duty on woollens is 100 per cent; their doty on cottons and textiles is over 50 per cent. As regards the duty on everything which they want to make and on which they fear the competition of Britain or Germany, they impose such a tariff that no imports appear on their list at all. To-day we import cloth in worsted and tweeds, about as many square yards as they import into the United States, because where we have a duty of 25 per cent, they have a duty that runs from 75 to 100 per cent. That is why that article does not appear to swell the amount of their imports.
But to go back to the development of Canada, we want a policy that will develop these industries, that will develop factories to manufacture these raw materials, that will protect the labouring men working in Canada, not unreasonably, not irrationally, but so as to give them a chance to carry on their business in this country. If that is done, as it may be done equitably, I believe the tariff board such as is asked for by the Trades and Labour Council, to act in an advisory capacity to the Minister or Acting Minister of Finance, will be found to be of great assistance. With such a policy, and with the wonderful natural resources of the country developed, then I think we should enter upon the era of prosperity that we are all looking for. It is true that the returns now show in certain respects that it is even coming upon us; there is a sign as though trade were now beginning to improve in this country. I always like to look at these situations in a hopeful way; I do not like the shadows in my path to be any that I cast myself, either from imagination or reality. I think that times are mending and business will improve; and such a tariff policy, so framed, so formed to protect labour and industry, would act wonderfully in the development and expansion of our trade, our factories and our natural resources.
