No matter how we may differ in our conclusions, from the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond), we' all listen with great interest to his addresses and we certainly agree that they are kindly and that the hon. member's earnestness for the city he represents would draw tears almost from the very stones themselves. However, what is the situation in Brantford? I am reminded that just a few weeks ago a certain delegation from the city of Brantford, including these very same implement manufacturers of which the hon. member has spoken and to whom he is so admirably loyal, arranged several meetings with different groups in this House including a number of representatives of the Progressive party; and the question occurred to me whether these implement manufacturers of Brantford were as loyal to the hon. member who represents them as he has been to them. To our surprise, after waiting for half an hour or more, the implement manufacturers from Brantford who were on this delegation failed to show up. However, a certain manufacturer from the city who undertook to speak for them stated their case, but I do not know that he succeeded in putting it very -well before us. Several questions were asked, among which were the following important queries: First of all, what is the condition of the different manufacturing concerns in Brantford, with special reference to the binder twine industry? To this question that gentleman was forced to confess that the binder twine industry, although on the free list and without any protection, was the only manufacturing concern in Brantford that was running on full shift and making full speed ahead. The question was next asked him: What is the problem of the manufacturers in the city of Brantford-is it a question of protection or one of lack of sales? Further, if any government in this country were to increase protection would it have the desired effect of giving impetus to the manufacture of implements in Brantford, or would it solve their problem? In reply to this question he was also obliged to confess that the problem was one of lack of sales and that not only would protection fail to solve it but that it would only aggravate the situation; in other words, if sales were the result of conditions favourable to buying, an increase in price due to increase in protection would simply aggravate the situation by reducing the purchasing power of the consumers. Now, there is a direct relation between the implement manufacturer and his purchaser, who in this case is the Canadian farmer; and the real problem is not so much one of protection as one of inadequate purchasing power 
on the part of the farmer. So that anything we can do in this House to increase that purchasing power will indirectly bring added prosperity to the manufacturer.
We have to-day been discussing in this House the fiscal policy brought down by this government, which has aroused unusual interest throughout the country. As the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson) showed this afternoon, while some two-thirds of the electors of this country supported in the last election candidates advocating a line of action similar to what is proposed in the policy of this budget we find that until now the government has taken little action in that direction. For two sessions in this House we have had budgets that have only made a gesture towards tariff reduction, and this is the first budget brought down by the present government that has actually budged. Because, therefore, this budget follows a line of action which we in this part of the House believe will not only promote the best interests of the agricultural community but will also improve the condition generally of the people of Canada, we feel more kindly towards it than we have done to any budget that has been presented to the people for several long years. While we can and do agree with our friends to the right that the reductions proposed by this budget may provide little immediate, relief to the producers of the country through the medium of the reduction on the implements of production, at the same time we deny that the proposed changes will have either the disastrous or even harmful effects upon the makers of these implements which some of our friends to the right prophesy. It is true that certain manufacturing concerns in this country are in a bad way financially. But the crying need of the Canadian manufacturer to-day is sales; his most remunerative matket is the home market, that is to say, Canada, and particularly agricultural Canada. His sales bear a direct relation to the purchasing power of his customer, who in the case of the implement manufacturer is the Canadian farmer. No group in this House is bold enough, facing conditions as they are, to suggest that the condition of the Canadian farmer is in any way bright; in fact, his purchasing power is extremely limited. And such being the accepted fact in regard to the condition of the customer, what is the proper course to pursue to provide the remedy? Some like the hon. member for Brantford would suggest more protection. But this, we believe, would only aggravate

The Budget-Mr. Brethen
the trouble. Higher protection, if it means anything, means the power to increase the selling price of the protected goods. Would anyone be bold enough to say that by raising the selling price we are going to make the purchaser buy more freely? Fifty years of this policy has proven the fallacy of attempting by such a system of taxation to make the country rich. I insist, Mr. Speaker, that you do not increase the taxable wealth of Canada by taxing a gentleman in East Peterborough and giving the benefit of that tax to a gentleman in Toronto. Such a course prevents the natural and honest distribution of wealth, but it does not create or augment wealth.
Let me illustrate the very important relation which exists between our producers and consumers. Last September I paid a visit to the western provinces, including British Columbia, and from Kamloops I took a motor drive of 370 miles through the Okanagan valley. There to my surprise I learned firsthand from the fruit growers that their condition was probably the most discouraging of that of any other producers in the Dominion. I was very sorry to learn this because the evidences of great production were to be found everywhere. One particular fruit grower told me he had cut down his peach orchard and was planting it with apples, and although the fruit was of immense size and quality only one-half of the peach crop would be harvested. He added that only one-half of the cherry crop had been harvested. In asking for an explanation I got the following, and I give it for what it is worth. I was told that the fruit industry in British Columbia was built up upon the prairie market when the prairies were in a more prosperous condition than they are to-day, and that when the purchasing power of the prairie farmer failed the result was instantly reflected in the returns to the fruit farmer of British Columbia. Talking to a man on the train who had some experience in growing fruit and also in selling it on the prairies, he told me: "It is just this way, when the prairie farmer is properous he does not go into a store and ask for one or two baskets of peaches, as you do in Ontario; he says to the storekeeper, "What are your peaches a crate today?" And upon being told the price he added: "I will take four or five crates.'" The fruit industry of British Columbia was evidently built up on that kind of market. But in a year like last, when in spite of a bumper crop, the largest in the history of Canada, he finds his cash returns depleted to the extent of seventy million dollars, somebody besides the farmer is going to feel it; it is going to be reflected in some other industries besides fanning, in fact it will be reflected in every industry of this country.
This question of sales has a very important bearing upon every industry. A week or so ago while I was down in the city of Halifax I noticed in one of the local papers this headline: "Cross Fertilizer Company Goes into Liquidation, due to the Reduction of the Tariff." I thought the budget was acting very quickly on the fertilizer industry, so I made inquiries. To my surprise I found the explanation given by the farmers was that for the past couple of years this particular company had been unable to sell their fertilizer because it was unsuitable, not being water soluble, and after the farmers had tried it and got no results they simply quit buying. Thereupon the fertilizer company went into liquidation not because of any lowering lor raising of the tariff, but simply because they were turning out a product which the farmers would not- buy. But see the camouflage of the situation!
I was interested to-night to hear the member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) refer to farm tractors. We hear in this House that the manufacture of tractors ceased in Brantford and in other manufacturing centres of Ontario because of the removal of the duty. I have often wondered' if that were really the explanation. In my trip through Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta last year I only once saw anything that looked1 like a tractor operating on summer fallow, and it was so far away that I could not be certain whether it was a tractor or not. I saw several threshing machines running,' but the great work of the tractor in past years on the prairies was conspicuous by its absence, the reason being not because in war time days the tractor was not considered a valuable asset to the farmers of the West, but because in these days when horse flesh is very cheap-practically unsaleable-when harness is cheaper and when horse feeds net the farmer little or nothing at his own barn, it does not pay him to operate tractors, and therefore the farmer has ceased to buy them. As the manager of the Brandon experimental farm expressed it to me, "We are past the tractor stage." The very fact that all the farmers of the West have ceased buying tractors would seem to me some explanation why the tractor industry in this country should cease-lack of sales. Possibly that had as much or greater influence on its cessation than the removal of the duty.
The Budget-Mr. Brethen

The prosperity of industrial Canada is certainly based upon the prosperity of agricultural Canada, and the sooner this truth is recognized the quicker 'will come that national prosperity we so fondly look for. Without any bitterness in my heart to our great industrial magnates, I am reminded that the present situation in which they find themselves, due to the lack of sales, in other words, due to the lack of purchasing power of their best customers, the Canadian farmers, is very largely the result of their action in 1911. In that year there was offered a market to the Canadian farmer that to-day the people very generally believe was a real market and would have meant very much in bettering our agricultural condition. But what did we find? At that time these very industrial magnates and financiers, although this was a question of reciprocity on natural products and, in a sense was none of their business, butted in and robbed the farmer of that market and of that industrial encouragement which would have been theirs. And so, to-day we find these very men, largely as a result of their action at that time virtually frying. in their fat. The crying need of the hour is to make the basic or primary industries of this country prosperous. Then general prosperity will follow as naturally as day follows night. By attempting to bridge the chasm between the high cost of everything which the farmer buys and the low price he receives for everything he has to sell, the government in this budget I believe has made an honest attempt to bring about better conditions and greater prosperity for the people of Canada. I am not one of those who have altogether lost faith in Canada. Neither do I belong to that cult in this House who seem to think because we have lost a good many real Canadians to the country to the south of us that we should advertise in this parliament to all the world that Canada is going to the bow-wows. I have here a letter from a young man who was employed for some years in the Civil Service and who a few weeks ago considered that he could better his condition by seeking employment in the great city of Detroit. After he had walked the streets of Detroit for two weeks he wrote imploring me to try and find him something in the way of a job. This is what he says: "Employment is very scarce here. Hundreds, yes thousands, walking the streets." This bears out the knowledge I have with regard to certain other young men who left our locality for different places in the States, very many of whom, at least fifty per cent, are 
now back home again because they could not get work. Some of them have already secured jobs of a permanent nature at home, which indicates that they have not the slightest intention of going south again to try their luck. I have here a clipping from the Toronto Globe of April 24 last:
The only large cities in the United States in which there is still an acute shortage of houses, accompanied by increasing rents, are Philadelphia, Chicago and Pittsburg. Canadian building trade mechanics who have been taking part in the building boom across the border will soon be coming home again.
I cannot help believing that much of the emphasis that has been placed on this emigration to the United States has been done purely from a partisan attempt to discredit the work of this government, and I would say that if the tariff policy of this government has had anything to do with sending these men to the States in the last two years, the onus must be shared equally by both the old parties because the present budget represents the first real distinction in the fiscal policy of the two old parties for several years.
I am about to ask a question that I wish I could answer: What is wrong with Canada? I think if some of the brightest minds in this House would pay to this question the attention it deserves, instead of wasting their efforts in fighting their election battles over again, it would be far more in the interest of Canada. What is wrong with Canada? The increase in the national debt from 8336,000,000 in 1913 to $2,453,000,000, which was the figure that the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) gave for 1923, cannot fail to mean increased taxation, and not only an increase in direct taxation but a much greater increase in indirect taxation, and this increase in indirect taxation I believe is reflected in the increased cost of distribution, in the increased cost of manufacture, in increased labour costs, rent costs, and so forth, which combined to bring about that very grave situation in Canada, the high cost of living. The protective tariff does not benefit the producer of our wheat, of our meats, our fish, or our cheese, because these products are sold in the markets of the world, and while a very large percentage of these products may be consumed in Canada it is the exportable surplus that sets the price. A lower cost of living is the only salvation for such a producer in the face of world competition.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this is the time for a national audit. Can we cut the cost of government, or the high cost of distribution that is throttling the very life of this country? Can our House of Commons and

The Budget-Mr. Brethen
mate be reduced to a size commensurate with our ability to pay? I believe that the co-ordination of portfolios, that of the Solicitor General with the Minister of Justice, for instance, is just as important as the co-ordination of railroads. I would also suggest to the government that the intent of the resolution of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) be put into effect, and the war time indemnity be reduced to harmonize with the present condition of affairs. Economy, like charity, should begin at home, and no strong appeal for economy in the country at large can come without the members of this House showing their willingness to blaze the trail by attacking their own purses. I, have heard it suggested in this connection that not merely the present indemnity but possibly an increased indemnity is necessary to attract the best men to this House. That I do not believe. I do not believe that the lure of the dollar will ever' in this country, or in any other country, appeal to the truly great man like the call to service. In coming up from Halifax with the rest of the Progressive members a week or so ago we had the good fortune to meet an Australian on the train, and upon our invitation he gave us a very interesting talk upon that dominion. He was well informed and I doubt if any press agent was better fitted for the task of placing his country in a good fight before the world at large. That experience made me think that probably we might follow the Australian gentleman's example and apply the same attitude to our own country. Let us have faith in Canada. Let us, if I may be allowed to use the term "Sell Canada to Canadians." I am not pessimistic enough to believe that because they have cheap labour in France, or Italy, or some other European countries that we cannot in Canada compete with it. As the Australian already referred to said, "In Italy they just muddle along in agriculture. The idea of one man leading a horse attached to a plough, and another man holding the plough handle!" And just such conditions as these render it impossible for European countries, even though they have cheap labour, to compete with the efficient agriculturists of Canada.	[DOT].
I believe that the greatest asset of the National railroads of Canada is the patriotic spirit of the people of the Dominion toward their own railway system. I quite agree with the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond), when he suggests that we should be 100 per cent Canadian, and whenever we can buy Canadian made goods at anything like the same price as foreign goods I believe we should do so. It will be this "get together spirit" on the part of the man on the farm, the man in the shop, and the man in the home to buy Canadian made goods-because they are the best and because they were produced by Canadians,-that is going to solve, or help very largely to solve, the financial and economic difficulties through which Canada is passing.
